summary: Describes a syntax for embedding S-HTTP negotiation parameters in HTML documents so that a web page can tell a browser how to set up secure exchanges. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A web page includes a note saying how to lock up the conversation before the browser starts.

subtitle: Adding S-HTTP security parameters to HTML anchors and documents.

tldr.problem: Web pages need a way to tell browsers what encryption and authentication to use when following links, but HTML has no syntax for embedding such security parameters.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2659 defines new HTML attributes for anchors (DN, NONCE, CRYPTOPTS) and new elements (CERTS and CRYPTOPTS) that carry S-HTTP security negotiation parameters.
tldr.outcome: Web pages can now instruct browsers on cryptographic settings, though this approach was never widely adopted and S-HTTP itself never became standard.

today: RFC 2659 is Experimental. S-HTTP never became standard, and HTTPS with TLS displaced the entire approach. Modern web security is handled at the transport layer by TLS negotiation, not by embedding instructions in HTML.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2659 describes a way to add security instructions to HTML documents. It builds on S-HTTP (Secure HyperText Transfer Protocol), defined in RFC 2660, which allows HTTP messages to be encrypted and authenticated with different cryptographic algorithms.

The problem RFC 2659 solves is that web pages need to tell browsers what cryptographic settings to use when following a hyperlink. Without this, the browser has no way to know what encryption method the destination server expects.
sections.eli5: When you click a link on a web page, the page might want to say: use this special kind of encryption for this link. RFC 2659 shows how.

sections.title: New HTML Attributes and Elements
sections.content:
The RFC defines three new attributes for HTML anchors and form submissions. DN specifies the distinguished name (the identity) of the server to encrypt the request for. NONCE is a unique value included in the request to prevent replay attacks. CRYPTOPTS lists cryptographic options such as which encryption algorithms are acceptable.

The RFC also introduces two new HTML elements. CERTS contains certificates (in PEM or PKCS-7 format) provided as advisory data for the browser. CRYPTOPTS elements define named groups of cryptographic options that anchors can reference.
sections.eli5: New instructions tell the browser: Who the server is, a unique code for this request, and how to encrypt it. You can also include certificates and encryption recipes.

sections.title: Usage Example
sections.content:
The RFC shows a concrete example: an HTML anchor with embedded certificate data and security parameters. The CERTS element near the top contains a certificate chain in PKCS-7 format (base64-encoded). The anchor itself specifies the server's distinguished name, which algorithms to use, and a hyperlink to an S-HTTP server.

The syntax uses SGML quoting conventions (such as " for quotation marks) to properly escape special characters in the embedded data.
sections.eli5: Here is how it looks: you put the server's certificate at the top, then the link tells the browser what encryption recipe to use when clicking it.

references.text: Rescorla, E. and A. Schiffman, "The Secure HyperText Transfer Protocol", RFC 2660, August 1999.
